submission.natural_language_explanation: L3/N997- is GELU's dip rather than a detector: its strength is -GELU(z) for a linear read z of the layer-3 residual, so the ceiling 0.170 is exactly GELU's global minimum (all twenty top examples are ties at that floor, 5,452 of 199,983 scanned tokens share the top histogram bin, and 28.8% of tokens clear the 0.25 active line), and a token reaches 0.10-0.17 when it is a mid-frequency English content word - a noun, verb or adjective such as ' risks', ' entropy', ' study', ' people', ' element' or ' quality' - read inside ordinary prose. Predict a probe ACTIVE when it contains at least one such content word in an ordinary clause, and INACTIVE only when every one of its tokens is a function word, pronoun, digit, operator or whitespace/newline (function-word strings, indented code, numeric tables); the passage's overall level rides a slowly varying contextual offset (lag-1 autocorrelation 0.64, 77% of the input attribution lying more than 16 tokens back, which source, language, position and register labels do not explain), so roughly a third of ordinary English sentences still fall below the line, and the peak does not move for any edit that leaves a dip-band token in place.

description: This document serves as a guide to getting started with RDF and ArangoDB. In it, we highlight some potential approaches for working with RDF graphs and then some of the considerations when attempting to bring RDF data into ArangoDB.
title: Mapping RDF data to ArangoDB Graphs
---
Mapping RDF data to ArangoDB Graphs
====================================

This document serves as a guide to getting started with 
[RDF](https://www.w3.org/TR/rdf11-concepts/){:target="_blank"} and ArangoDB. In it 
we highlight some potential approaches for working with RDF graphs and then some 
of the considerations when attempting to bring RDF data into ArangoDB. The 
concept of working with RDF graphs in ArangoDB is not fully supported, but we 
would like to start introducing solutions for mapping and start the conversation 
with the community. We welcome any feedback from the community on ways to
improve the ingestion of RDF graphs as we work on an official implementation for
ArangoDB. You can accomplish a lot with ArangoDB and RDF with a few workarounds,
depending on your needs but be sure to see the caveats section for some
considerations.

Getting Started
---------------

RDF graphs are purely directed graphs with no properties on vertices or edges. In
RDF, everything is referenced by edges; these edges are known as statements.
Statements are in the form `[subject, predicate, object, [graph]].` Statements pose 
an interesting challenge when trying to interpolate an RDF graph as a property 
graph. ArangoDB is uniquely suited to handle this due to having edges which 
have a similar structure to vertices and thus can be used to resemble an 
RDF graph or to instead represent RDF statements as properties associated 
with a `subject.` For this discussion, it is helpful to have an example; the
following is a simple RDF graph for Sir Arthur Conan Doyle.

```XML
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<rdf:RDF
   xmlns:rdf="http://www.w3.org/1999/02/22-rdf-syntax-ns#"
>
  <rdf:Description rdf:about="http://dbpedia.org/resource/Arthur_Conan_Doyle">
    <rdf:type rdf:resource="http://dbpedia.org/ontology/Person"/>
    <rdf:type rdf:resource="http://dbpedia.org/ontology/Writer"/>
    <rdf:type rdf:resource="http://www.w3.org/2002/07/owl#Thing"/>
    <rdf:type rdf:resource="http://dbpedia.org/ontology/Artist"/>
  </rdf:Description>
</rdf:RDF>
```

The above code is RDF in
[RDF/XML](https://www.w3.org/TR/rdf-syntax-grammar/){:target="_blank"} format.
This syntax can be considered the original/standard RDF syntax. However, many
different serializations exist, and thanks to their readability and ease of
parsing, has grown in popularity.

Q:

could vs might, different or same

Is the difference between could and might in a) much more significant than in b)?
a) You need to discuss with them how they could vs might help you.
b) You could vs might try calling the help desk.
Can we put might=would perhaps in a)?

A:

a) You need to discuss with them how they could help you.

This would imply the question, "Do they have the ability or capacity to help you?"

a) You need to discuss with them how they might help you.

This implies that they have the ability, but the question is, "In what ways may they help you?"

b) You could/might try calling the help desk.

In this instance, the implied meanings are similar enough to be almost identical; the difference, however would be in the tone--"could" implying a simple suggestion or even a mild command, while "might" is a polite suggestion with no implied command.

Can we put might=would perhaps in a)?

I wouldn't. The phrase "would perhaps" is unnecessarily wordy and weak.

The drink gained popularity in the United States in 2009. Varieties of the beverage were served in regions including Colorado, Florida, Maine, Massachusetts, Missouri, Oregon, and Virginia. It has also achieved notice in Canada and the United Kingdom.

On the first warm morning of April, the market in the old town opens before the sun clears the hills. Farmers arrive with crates of young lettuce, bundles of thyme, and jars of dark honey, and they set them on tables that have stood in the same square for a hundred years. The baker, who has risen at four, hands out warm loaves to the people already waiting, and the smell of the bread drifts past the fountain and mixes with the smoke of a small fire where someone is roasting chestnuts. Children run between the stalls while their parents argue about the price of cheese, and an old woman in a blue coat sells bunches of yellow flowers that she cut from her own garden the night before. Nobody hurries. The morning belongs to the square, and the square belongs to the town.

By noon the light has grown hard and the square is crowded. A musician with a worn guitar sits on the steps of the church and plays songs that the older people remember from their youth; a few of them sing along, quietly, and one man closes his eyes as if he were hearing something he had lost. The fishmonger shouts across the noise of the crowd, holding up a silver trout, and a boy carries a bucket of ice past the vegetable stands. Everywhere there is the low, constant talk of the market, a sound that seems to have its own weather, rising and falling with the hour.

Later, when the stalls begin to close and the crates are stacked again in the trucks, the town returns to its ordinary quiet. The fountain keeps running, the pigeons return to the stones, and the last of the light falls across the empty tables. Someone sweeps the square with a long broom, and the dust rises and settles. It is a small place, and its life is small, but on a morning like this it feels complete: the bread, the flowers, the argument over cheese, the songs that the old people still remember. Nothing important happens, and that is the point. The market will open again on Thursday, and the people will come, and the square will hold them.
